questions.question: In a metric space $(\boldsymbol{X},d)$, what makes $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ an interior point of $\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq\boldsymbol{X}$?
options: Every ball around $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ contains a point outside $\boldsymbol{E}$.
There exists $\varepsilon \gt 0$ such that $\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,\varepsilon)\subseteq\boldsymbol{E}$.
$\boldsymbol{x}_0$ is outside $\boldsymbol{E}$.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ contains exactly one point.

questions.question: What notation is used for the set of interior points of $\boldsymbol{E}$?
options: $\partial\boldsymbol{E}$
$\operatorname{int}\,\boldsymbol{E}$
$\overline{\boldsymbol{E}}$
$\boldsymbol{E}^{-1}$

questions.question: For $E = (0,1)\subseteq\mathbb{R}$, which point is an interior point of $E$?
For $E = \{1,2,3\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ with the usual metric, which statement is correct?
options: Every point of $E$ is an interior point.
Only $1$ is an interior point.
Only $2$ is an interior point.
No point of $E$ is an interior point.

questions.question: Why must an interior point of $\boldsymbol{E}$ belong to $\boldsymbol{E}$?
options: Because every ball centred at $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ contains $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ itself.
Because interior points are defined to be outside the set.
Because $\varepsilon$ must be equal to $0$.
Because all subsets of a metric space are open.

questions.question: How is the interior of $\boldsymbol{E}$ characterised among open subsets of $\boldsymbol{E}$?
options: It is the smallest closed subset of $\boldsymbol{E}$.
It is always equal to the whole metric space $\boldsymbol{X}$.
It is always empty.
It is the largest open subset of $\boldsymbol{E}$.

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}$ with the usual metric, what is $\operatorname{int}[0,1]$?
options: $\varnothing$

questions.question: If $\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,0.2)\subseteq\boldsymbol{E}$, what can be concluded about $\boldsymbol{x}_0$?
options: $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ is not in $\boldsymbol{E}$.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ has no interior points.
$\boldsymbol{x}_0$ is an interior point of $\boldsymbol{E}$.
$\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,0.2)$ must be empty.

questions.question: A student checks only that $\boldsymbol{x}_0\in\boldsymbol{E}$. Why is this insufficient to prove that $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ is interior?
options: One must also find a positive-radius ball around $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ contained in $\boldsymbol{E}$.
Membership in $\boldsymbol{E}$ is never relevant.
The definition requires a negative radius.
Interior points must lie outside every open ball centred at a point of $\boldsymbol{E}$.

questions.question: Which statement correctly links interior points with open metric balls?
options: The same radius must work for every subset of $\boldsymbol{X}$.
Only radius $1$ is allowed.
The ball must contain all of $\boldsymbol{X}$.
The radius may depend on the point $\boldsymbol{x}_0$.

questions.question: For $E = [0,1)\subseteq\mathbb{R}$, which point is not an interior point of $E$?
Suppose $\operatorname{int}\,\boldsymbol{E} = \varnothing$. Which conclusion is justified?
options: $\boldsymbol{E}$ has no point with a positive-radius ball contained in $\boldsymbol{E}$.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ must be the empty set, as it has no interior points at all.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ must be finite, like the set $\{1,2,3\}$ in $\mathbb{R}$.
Every point of $\boldsymbol{E}$ is an exterior point of $\boldsymbol{E}$.

questions.question: Which condition makes $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ an interior point of $\boldsymbol{E}$?
options: There exists $\varepsilon \gt 0$ such that $\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,\varepsilon)\subseteq \boldsymbol{E}$.
Every ball around $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ contains a point outside $\boldsymbol{E}$.
$\boldsymbol{x}_0$ is a boundary point of $\boldsymbol{E}$.
$\boldsymbol{x}_0\notin \boldsymbol{E}$.

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}$, which point is in $\operatorname{int}[0,1]$?
Why does an interior point necessarily lie in the set?
options: Because every point of the ambient space is an interior point of every set.
Because interior points are excluded from the set.
Because every ball centred at that point contains the centre point itself.
Because negative radii are allowed.

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}$ with the usual metric, which point is interior to $E=(0,1)$?
In $\mathbb{R}$ with the usual metric, which set is $\operatorname{int}[0,1]$?
options: $\varnothing$

questions.question: Why is $1$ not an interior point of $\{1,2,3\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}$?
options: The point $1$ is not an element of the set.
Every open ball around $1$ contains real numbers not in $\{1,2,3\}$.
The set contains too many points.
The point $1$ is larger than all elements of the set.

questions.question: How is the interior of $\boldsymbol{E}$ related to open subsets of $\boldsymbol{E}$?
options: It is the smallest closed set containing $\boldsymbol{E}$.
It is the largest open subset of $\boldsymbol{E}$.
It is always equal to the boundary of $\boldsymbol{E}$.
It is always empty unless $\boldsymbol{E}$ is finite.

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}$ with the usual metric, what is $\operatorname{int}((0,1]\cup\{2\})$?
